transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-05-14 15:00 PDT
Duration: 57 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Alex (Redwood SE), Dr. Lena Ortiz (Head of ML, Omegasoft), Rajesh Iyer (SRE), Marta Gomez (Product)

Summary: Quick alignment on prefix/prompt caching strategy for multi-tenant inference. Primary focus: cache key design, consistent hashing, TTL/expiry, safety/tenant isolation, on-prem VPC constraints, and how quantization/batching affect hit rates and latency.

Topics: prefix key entropy, multi-tenant namespace isolation, eviction policies, cache warming, batching windows, int8 quantization perf trade-offs, network e2e latency in VPCs.

[00:00] Maya (Redwood): hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'll kick off — quick introductions, then alex will walk through the cache design patterns we've seen in similar customers.
[00:18] Dr. Lena: yeah thanks maya, we have about 45 minutes of technical — we want to make sure this maps to our SLOs. our p95 latency target is 120ms for short completion flows, and typical prompt length is about 80 tokens.
[00:32] Alex (Redwood SE): got it, that's helpful. quick clarifying q — when you say "short completion" is that user typing-autocomplete style or a system prompt chain?
[00:38] Dr. Lena: mostly user-facing autocomplete, some template prompts for billing summaries, so there's a lot of repeated prefixes.
[00:45] Rajesh: and from infra we need a design that respects tenant isolation — we can't let one noisy tenant evict others' cached prefixes. we run multi-az clusters in our VPC and want the option to run on-prem later.
[00:59] Alex (Redwood SE): okay. couple of high-level options: namespace-per-tenant keys, or a global namespace with tenant-id baked into the cache key. we usually prefer the former for safety but the latter can save memory if you shard by consistent-hash ring.
[01:20] Marta: sorry can you unpack "consistent-hash ring" — is that the same as sticky routing?
[01:25] Alex: similar idea — you pick a hash over tenant+prefix and map it to a shard. sticky routing pins requests to the same node which helps local cache hits, consistent hashing helps when nodes are added/removed without rebalancing everything.
[01:37] Dr. Lena: what's our expected hit-rate deltas between namespace-per-tenant vs global with tenant ids?
[01:43] Alex: rough rule of thumb: if tenants are relatively small and prefixes overlap a lot, global with tenant id yields higher overall hit-rate because popular prefixes across tenants share cache entries if you intentionally avoid tenant separation. but if cross-tenant sharing is forbidden for compliance, namespace-per-tenant is required and hit-rates drop proportionally. realistic delta for Omegasoft-like traffic — maybe 8-20% hit-rate reduction for strict isolation, depends on prefix entropy.
[02:03] Rajesh: cross-tenant sharing is a no-go for us on production PII paths. we need cryptographic separation.
[02:10] Alex: understood. then the question becomes how to reduce the hit-rate loss: we can do intra-tenant caching plus a small global 'public' cache for non-PII templates, or we can use a two-layer cache: fast local per-tenant LRU + shared cold-storage cache on SSD.
[02:28] Dr. Lena: two-layer sounds interesting. what's the complexity and latency overhead?
[02:33] Alex: local LRU in memory is sub-ms. fallback to shared SSD adds ~5-12ms depending on topology. if you have network hop inside VPC between AZs it could be more. for on-prem it depends on your network fabric.
[02:47] Maya: also note our KV cache supports prefix chunking and K/V fingerprinting — i.e., we store short key IDs for long prompts to reduce memory. that helps with high-entropy prefixes.
[02:58] Dr. Lena: what's "prefix chunking" in practice?
[03:01] Alex: split long prefixes into hashed tokens and store a final combined fingerprint; this avoids storing full string keys for all historical prefixes. it's lossy for collision risk but we engineer collision thresholds low. we can share code snippets.
[03:15] [03:15] Rajesh: quick practical q — how do you recommend TTL policies? our user flows where prefix reuse decays after 72 hours, but some templates are evergreen.
[03:27] Alex: recommend hybrid TTLs: tenant-configurable. default sliding expiry of 24 hours for user-driven prefixes, and pinned TTL infinite for known templates (explicitly flagged). sliding expiry helps with bursty traffic and warms back up automatically.
[03:41] Dr. Lena: will sliding expiry blow up eviction storms?
[03:45] Alex: it can if many keys are refreshed synchronously. mitigation: add jitter to expiry and use probabilistic early-LRU eviction to smooth peaks. also pre-warming for expected traffic after deployments.
[03:58] Marta: pre-warming — can you do that automatically from traces?
[04:02] Alex: yes, Redwood Optimize can ingest a trace and suggest top-k prefixes to warm or push to a hot cache layer. we built a small tool that converts top N prefixes into warm-up requests on fleet startup. we'll share the script.
[04:18] [04:18] Dr. Lena: on isolation: we must prove no accidental cross-tenant leakage. how do you audit that?
[04:25] Alex: two mechanisms: tenant-id included in the key and request-level logging, plus a cryptographic namespacing option — HMAC the key with tenant-specific key (from customer KMS) so even identical prefixes yield different cache keys across tenants. we also emit audit events for cache hits/misses with tenant IDs.
[04:43] Rajesh: the HMAC approach sounds good, but will HMAC slow down hashing?
[04:47] Alex: HMAC adds CPU but it's small relative to token generation. you can do an HMAC once at ingress and store the derived short key in a local fast store. we also support hardware-accelerated crypto via HSM/KMS in private deployments.
[05:00] Maya: quick tangent on quantization — Lena you mentioned models sometimes run int8 in staging. question is whether quantization changes cacheability?
[05:10] Dr. Lena: yes some variations in output distribution happen with int8; for short prefixes it could change completions slightly and thus cache hits are less likely if you cache outputs vs cache embeddings for rerank.
[05:22] Alex: recommended pattern: cache model *states* or partial KV caches (i.e., cached key-value attention states) rather than final decoded tokens when safe; that preserves reuse across small model variant changes. but storing KV states is larger in memory and architecture-specific.
[05:38] Marta: storing KV states — that ties us closely to model versions, is that manageable?
[05:42] Alex: yes you tag cached KV with model id and quantization flag. on model change, you can either invalidate or keep both and route by model id. Redwood's rollout supports fallback to older model if cache warming is needed.
[05:56] [05:56] Dr. Lena: about consistent hashing — if we have 12 shards should we aim for replication factor >1 to protect cold misses during rolling deployments?
[06:04] Alex: yes, we recommend replication factor 2 for production to minimize misses when nodes are drained. consistent hashing with virtual nodes eases balance. we also support range-based sharding for locality if you want tenant affinity by region.
[06:18] Rajesh: any known gotchas with virtual nodes and latency tail?
[06:22] Alex: virtual nodes increase routing table size but reduce imbalance; tail latency usually comes from cross-AZ lookups — prefer to route to local AZ's shards when possible. also monitor per-shard hit-rate.
[06:36] [06:36] Dr. Lena: network e2e: in our VPC we have firewall inspection that can add ~3-7ms. how do you factor that into our p95?
[06:45] Maya: we run e2e tests that include network proxies, and Redwood's latency SLOs are configurable per-deployment. for on-prem we'd want a small perf trial to measure real numbers.
[06:55] Alex: for micro-optimizations: enable prefix-level caching at the gateway (edge) for the absolutely hot prefixes to shave off network hops.
[07:06] Marta: what about batching? we need throughput for analytics endpoints that do large bulk requests — batching increases throughput but increases per-request latency.
[07:16] Alex: yes, tradeoff: batching raises token-per-second throughput drastically. for user interactive endpoints we keep batch windows tight (5-10ms) or use immediate non-batched pathways. for bulk analytics, use larger batch sizes and asynchronous APIs. Redwood supports dynamic batching and priority lanes.
[07:31] Dr. Lena: curious how batching interacts with cache hits — if one request in batch hits cached KV, do you short-circuit the whole batch?
[07:40] Alex: we can do per-request routing within a batch: the runtime can detect cache hits and only execute the missing items, but that complicates GPU kernel scheduling. often we pre-unbatch cache hits at the dispatcher and only send the non-hit items to GPU, which retains latency benefits.
[07:56] [07:56] Rajesh: fallback policies — if Dedicated capacity is exhausted do you have automatic fallback to hosted variants?
[08:02] Maya: yes, Redwood can configure policy-based fallbacks by model family. for on-prem strict air-gap deployments we don't automatically fallback unless customer enables a secure routing path.
[08:14] Dr. Lena: security: we'll need SOC2 docs, and for on-prem we require KMS integration and audit logs for cache access. do you support HSM-backed keys?
[08:25] Alex: yes, private deployments can integrate with customer HSM/KMS. cache keys can be derived with tenant-specific secrets so raw prefixes never leave the tenant boundary in plaintext in shared caches. audit logs are emitted with per-key metadata.
[08:40] Marta: do you support per-tenant RBAC over cache operations? e.g., only SRE can flush their tenant's cache?
[08:46] Maya: yes, console has per-tenant permissions and API tokens can be scoped. flush operations are logged and can be gated via approval workflows.
[08:56] [08:56] Dr. Lena: on observability — what metrics should we instrument?
[09:00] Alex: per-tenant hit-rate, per-shard latency, eviction rate, collision rate (if using fingerprinting), and memory pressure. also track model-id mismatch hits to detect when quantization changes are causing misses.
[09:13] Rajesh: collision rate — can you explain how you measure that?
[09:16] Alex: we track key fingerprint collisions heuristically by sampling keys and checking for same hash but differing payloads, plus bloom filters for quick detection. collisions should be negligible with 128-bit fingerprints.
[09:29] [09:29] Marta: operational question: when we do rolling updates of the runtime, what's recommended strategy to avoid thundering herd on cache misses?
[09:36] Alex: blue-green or canary with cache warming. if you scale down old nodes too fast you lose cached prefixes. recommended: keep a small percentage warm, and pre-populate new nodes with top-N prefixes before routing traffic.
[09:50] Dr. Lena: will warming increase cost significantly?
[09:53] Alex: small cost: it's just a set of synthetic requests to warm memory; the operational cost is tiny compared to cold token compute.
[09:59] [09:59] Rajesh: are there size limits for storing KV states? if we store kv for many tenants will memory explode?
[10:05] Alex: yes, KV states are large — roughly O(seq_len * hidden_dim) per cached state. we recommend storing KV only for extremely high-QPS hot prefixes (top 1-2%). for others store condensed partial outputs or final tokens. and we provide configurable quotas per-tenant.
[10:22] Maggie (off-record): [crosstalk]
[10:25] Alex: (laughs) okay — new question: what's your expected weekly QPS in peak?
[10:30] Dr. Lena: at peak about 11k reqs/min across all tenants, 60% are short completion paths.
[10:36] Alex: good — that's within a typical Dedicated pool. we'll propose a Dedicated config with a hot cache layer plus an optional SSD-backed shared layer.
[10:44] [10:44] Dr. Lena: on data residency — some of our EU customers need data to remain in EU. can you pin cache shards to region?
[10:50] Maya: yes, Redwood supports regional sharding and data residency controls; we can route EU traffic to EU-only shards and disable cross-region replication for those tenants.
[11:00] Marta: ROI question — what's expected token-cost reduction from prefix caching?
[11:05] Alex: depends on hit-rate. ballpark: a 30-40% hit-rate for the short completion workload could yield 20-30% reduction in token compute costs. with KV-state caching for the top 1% prefixes, that delta can be much larger.
[11:19] [11:19] Dr. Lena: what about auditability for cache purges? we need to show proof for compliance audits that a purge was performed.
[11:25] Alex: purge operations produce signed audit records including pre/post counts, affected keys (hashed), and actor who initiated. for private deployments these records can be shipped to your SIEM.
[11:39] Rajesh: any performance impact from continuous encryption at rest for cache layers?
[11:44] Alex: minimal for in-memory caches; for SSD-backed caches there is some CPU overhead for encryption but it's typically minor. we recommend mTLS for in-transit and envelope encryption for at-rest with HSM for private deployments.
[11:58] [11:58] Marta: about collision and privacy — if we fingerprint keys, is there risk that those fingerprints can be reversed?
[12:03] Alex: fingerprints are non-reversible if using a cryptographic hash salted per-tenant; if salted with tenant secret it's safe. unsalted / short fingerprints risk rainbow attacks. use HMAC with tenant secret when privacy required.
[12:18] Dr. Lena: okay — let's talk about a concrete pilot plan. what would you need from us?
[12:24] Alex: sample traces (anonymized prefix logs), target SLOs, a small cluster to run a load test, and security contact for KMS integration.
[12:31] Dr. Lena: we'll provide traces and SLO doc. can you also provide sample scripts to simulate sliding expiry and jitter?
[12:38] Alex: yes, will include that in the artifacts we send.
[12:41] [12:41] Maya: quick recap — next steps we covered: artifacts (cache key patterns doc, warming script), benchmark run by Alex, pricing and security docs by me, pilot scheduling. anything else?
[12:52] Dr. Lena: add quantization perf summary please.
[12:54] Maya: noted.
[12:56] [12:56] Rajesh: one last nit — in our compliance environment we cannot run any global cache that holds PII even transiently. solution?
[13:03] Alex: two options: don't cache PII prefixes (filter upstream), or use ephemeral per-tenant encrypted caches that are zeroed after TTL and use HSM-wrapped keys so even a snapshot is useless without tenant key.
[13:18] Marta: ok good — we'll make that part of the pilot acceptance criteria.
[13:23] Maya: great, thank you all. we'll push the docs after this call and set the follow up.
[13:28] Dr. Lena: thanks, bye.

Auto-summary (generated):
- Need tenant safe cache key design (HMAC salted keys recommended)
- Recommend two-layer caching: per-tenant in-memory LRU + shared SSD hot layer for non-PII templates

- Replication factor >=2 and consistent hashing with virtual nodes for resilience
- KV-state caching for top hot prefixes; tag with model+quantization id
